raw_record.support_text: A clinical (Phase II) study of cis-4-hydroxy-L-proline (CHP) in bladder and prostate cancer patients showed no adverse effects on liver parameters ALAT, ASAT, gamma-glutamyltransferase, and alkaline phosphatase after administration of 8 g CHP/day, 4 days/week for 3 weeks. The authors conclude that CHP had no adverse effects on liver function in humans, providing an explicit agent-specific negative for CHP hepatotoxicity; a rat hepatocyte culture model had predicted toxic effects.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Bladder and prostate cancer patient population
raw_record.extra_details: Dose 8 g/day, 4 days/week for 3 weeks; liver parameters assessed were ALAT, ASAT, gamma-glutamyltransferase and alkaline phosphatase; no adverse effects on any of these parameters. The negative conclusion refers to liver-test parameters in a Phase II clinical study, in contrast to a rat study showing ALAT/ASAT elevations.

raw_record.support_text: In all subjects treated with vilaprisan in phase I and II studies, no relevant changes in liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP, γ-GT, bilirubin) were observed, and serum liver enzyme level assessment indicated no safety concerns. The authors state that none of the known risk factors for drug-induced liver injury were found applicable to vilaprisan, concluding an explicit negative for vilaprisan-related human DILI.
raw_record.extra_details: No relevant changes in AST, ALT, ALP, γ-GT, or bilirubin across phase I and II studies. No applicable DILI risk factors reported: no inhibition of bile-acid transporters or bilirubin metabolism, no structural alerts leading to reactive intermediates or covalent binding, no mechanism-based CYP enzyme inhibition, no mitochondrial or other cell toxicity. A very low efficacious dose of 2-4 mg.

raw_record.support_text: Because of concerns about possible hepatotoxic reactions associated with naltrexone use, end-point aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels were examined. Naltrexone-treated subjects had significantly lower aspartate aminotransferase levels than placebo-treated subjects (F[1,72]=4.99, P<.05), with a similar trend noted for alanine aminotransferase (F[1,71]=2.96, P<.10). The mean (±SE) aspartate aminotransferase level for naltrexone-treated patients was 23.6±4.3 compared with 37.8±4.6 for placebo-treated patients.
raw_record.extra_details: 12-week randomized trial in alcohol-dependent patients (n=97). End-point AST levels were significantly lower in naltrexone-treated versus placebo-treated subjects, indicating no evidence of naltrexone-induced hepatotoxicity; higher liver enzyme levels were instead associated with coping skills/relapse prevention therapy assignment. Mean (±SE) ALT and AST for coping skills/relapse prevention groups were 44.2±4.8 and 37.7±4.5 versus 29.5±4.8 and 23.8±4.4 for supportive therapy groups.

raw_record.support_text: Preclinical and clinical data suggest that pretreatment with high doses of dexamethasone does not affect trabectedin efficacy but protects against trabectedin-induced hepatic injury, possibly by decreasing hepatic exposure to trabectedin through strong induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4, the isoenzyme primarily responsible for trabectedin elimination. In a phase II clinical trial in adult patients with recurrent advanced soft tissue sarcoma, co-treatment with dexamethasone improved the safety of trabectedin by reducing drug-induced hepatotoxicity. The trabectedin SmPC requires dexamethasone 20 mg i.v. 30 min before each trabectedin administration to provide a hepatoprotective effect.
raw_record.extra_details: Trabectedin (ET-743) is an anticancer agent used in advanced soft tissue sarcoma and ovarian carcinoma. Dexamethasone co-treatment in the phase II trial increased total body clearance by 28% and decreased half-life by 21% versus placebo; hepatic protection possibly via CYP3A4 induction. The paper also documents hepatic damage indicators (ALT/AST and bilirubin/AP elevations) across clinical studies (e.g., ALT/AST elevation all grades up to ~98%, with grade 3-4 elevations), and reviewed trial/reference data (RS[44], [10], [45], RS[46], [13], [47], RS[48], [9], [12]).; additional_details: None

raw_record.support_text: The main toxic side effect associated with isoniazid chemoprophylaxis is the development of hepatitis. A US study of nearly 14,000 persons between 1971 and 1972 (Kopanoff et al., 1978) found an overall rate of isoniazid-induced hepatitis of 1%, which was age-related (no cases in those aged <20 years, 2.3% in those aged >50 years) and also related to alcohol consumption.

Overall rate of isoniazid-induced hepatitis 1%; age-related with no cases under 20 years and 2.3% in persons >50 years; development of hepatitis also related to alcohol consumption. Discussed in the context of isoniazid preventive therapy for TB.

raw_record.support_text: Methotrexate at low doses used for psoriasis and other autoimmune diseases produced an unacceptably high incidence of hepatic toxicity in psoriatic patients receiving chronic treatment. In a series of 104 patients treated for a mean duration of 3.4 years with doses of 20 to 25 mg/wk, 23% showed significant pathologic changes (cirrhosis or active hepatitis) on liver biopsy. The toxicity was attributed to intrahepatic accumulation because methotrexate, a folate analogue, is concentrated in the liver, whereas once-weekly dosing reduced the incidence. The frequency of methotrexate hepatic toxicity is higher in psoriasis and low in rheumatoid arthritis, possibly reflecting differences in risk factors such as alcohol use, diabetes mellitus, and obesity.

raw_record.support_text: The study examined 25 Caucasian patients with minocycline DILI enrolled in DILIN prospective and retrospective studies. 80% were female, median age 19 years, and median latency from drug start to DILI onset was 318 days; 76% had acute hepatocellular liver injury with median ALT 1077 U/L (range 63-2333), median bilirubin 4.5 mg/dl, and 90% had a positive ANA. 50% were treated with corticosteroids and no subjects died or required liver transplant. The clinical features, including systemic arthralgias and autoantibodies in young women, are consistent with minocycline as a cause of DILI presenting with prominent autoimmune features.

Genetic analysis found a significant association between HLA-B*35:02 and minocycline-DILI risk, with 16% carrier frequency in cases vs 0.6% in population controls (Odds Ratio 29.6, 95% CI 7.8-89.8, p=2.5x10^-8), confirmed by sequence-based HLA typing; in silico modeling suggested direct binding of minocycline to this HLA risk allele may be an initiating event. Manuscript pair PMID 28323125 describes genetic determinants rather than a new causal drug.

raw_record.support_text: Isoniazid is identified as one of the NAT-sensitive drugs that is itself hepatotoxic. The causative role of isoniazid in cases of severe hepatic injury was established in a population study in the 1970s. Early claims that rapid acetylators are more susceptible to hepatotoxicity were refuted. In Japanese patients a significant association between hepatotoxicity and NAT2 genotype was observed under combined treatment with isoniazid–rifampicin, with relative risks of 4.0 and 28.0 for intermediate and slow acetylators versus rapid acetylators. The main risk factors for isoniazid-related hepatitis are prior viral infection by hepatitis B or C and HIV.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Hepatotoxicity highest risk with concurrent prior hepatitis B or C infection or HIV; a genotype-association analysis was performed under combined treatment with isoniazid–rifampicin.
raw_record.extra_details: Severity described as severe hepatic injury. Early claim that rapid acetylators are more susceptible to hepatotoxicity was refuted. In Japanese patients under isoniazid–rifampicin combination, relative risk of hepatotoxicity for intermediate and slow acetylators versus rapid acetylators was 4.0 and 28.0 respectively. Acetylhydrazine and hydrazine are possible candidates for the toxic metabolite mediating isoniazid toxicity. In patients with liver disease reports show decreased acetylation ratios or prolonged half-life; the prolongation may be quantitatively less important than underlying genetic differences. Rapid-acetylator genotype with abnormal liver function can yield incorrect phenotype classification. Hepatotoxicity noted as a major concern in antituberculosis treatment.

raw_record.support_text: Overstreet et al. present a case of fatal, progressive hepatotoxicity in a patient treated with lamotrigine. After presenting with a rash and fever, the patient developed elevated liver function tests and clinical sequelae of hepatic failure. Serial liver biopsies documented a subacute course: the initial biopsy showed approximately 50% hepatocyte necrosis, and a post mortem examination 3 weeks later displayed massive hepatic necrosis with extensive bile duct proliferation. Although the patient was taking other antipsychotics, the clinical course best parallels other reports of lamotrigine-associated hepatotoxicity.

raw_record.support_text: In Case 3, a 63-year-old woman treated with papaverine 80 mg four times a day for basilar-artery insufficiency developed a marked increase in SGOT, SGPT, and alkaline phosphatase after 5 weeks of treatment, plus burning epigastric pain; symptoms resolved on withdrawal and recurred on rechallenge with papaverine. In Case 4, a 54-year-old woman treated with papaverine 80 mg four times a day developed rising SGOT and SGPT after 18-23 days, and rechallenge with papaverine produced anorexia and vomiting. The authors conclude in the discussion that an intimate connection between papaverine administration and hepatopathy was demonstrated in these cases despite no prior reports of papaverine hepatotoxicity; liver biopsy in Case 3 showed foci of necrotic liver cells with inflammatory infiltration including eosinophilic granulocytes and bile staining of liver cells.
raw_record.extra_details: Case 3: 80 mg q.i.d., latency 5 weeks, concurrent marked SGOT/SGPT and alkaline phosphatase elevation, burning epigastric pain, symptom recurrence on rechallenge and resolution within 24 h of withdrawal, normal cholecystography; biopsy showed preserved lobular structure, focal necrotic liver cells with pyknotic nuclei and karyorrhexis, focal granulocyte infiltration, Kupffer-cell hyperplasia, periportal inflammation with eosinophilic granulocytes, and centrilobular bile staining with rare minimal bile thrombi. Case 4: 80 mg q.i.d., SGOT/SGPT rose slightly at day 18 and were clearly pathologic at day 23; rechallenge with only half a day of papaverine caused anorexia and one episode of vomiting. Discussion notes no previous animal or human reports of papaverine hepatotoxicity; no previous liver disease or hemolytic tendency in either patient.

raw_record.support_text: In a pharmacogenomic study of 148 pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) patients treated with methotrexate in the consolidation therapy phase, the AA genotype of the SLC19A1 c.80 variant was reported as a predictor of methotrexate-related hepatotoxicity. The paper frames hepatotoxicity as an adverse reaction arising from methotrexate therapy.
raw_record.qualifying_conditions: Pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia patients during the consolidation therapy phase (BFM protocol).
raw_record.extra_details: 148 patients analyzed; the AA genotype of SLC19A1 c.80 variant predicted methotrexate-related hepatotoxicity; the study assessed pharmacogenomic markers of methotrexate response and toxicity.
